patient.chief_complaint: Woke up with slurred speech and left arm clumsiness
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Lucia Mendoza is a 58-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a who presents to the emergency department after waking up at approximately 06:30 this morning with slurred speech and difficulty using her left hand. She reports going to bed at approximately 23:00 last night feeling entirely normal. She woke once around 03:00 to use the bathroom and states she felt fine at that time, though she acknowledges she was groggy and did not perform any fine motor tasks. When she woke at 06:30 for work, she noticed her speech sounded thick and her left hand was clumsy when she tried to button her shirt. She initially attributed this to sleeping on her arm but became concerned when the symptoms persisted after thirty minutes. She drove herself to a nearby urgent care center, which immediately redirected her to our emergency department via ambulance. EMS noted mild dysarthria, subtle left facial droop, and mild left upper extremity weakness on initial evaluation and activated a stroke alert. Fingerstick glucose in the field was 142 mg/dL. The patient arrived in the ED at 08:15. She denies any headache, visual changes, nausea, vomiting, seizure activity, or loss of consciousness. She reports no recent illness, fever, chest pain, or palpitations. She has been compliant with her medications but admits her blood pressure is often elevated when checked at the pharmacy. She also acknowledges that she has not been using her CPAP machine for the past several months because it makes her uncomfortable. Her last known well time is conservatively estimated at 23:00 the prior evening, approximately 9 hours and 15 minutes before ED arrival, placing her outside the standard IV alteplase window. However, her self-reported bathroom visit at 03:00 raises the possibility that symptoms began after that time, though this cannot be confirmed.

results.title: MRI-Guided Thrombolysis for Stroke with Unknown Time of Onset (WAKE-UP Trial)
results.authors: Thomalla G, Simonsen CZ, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase improved functional outcome in wake-up stroke patients selected by DWI-FLAIR mismatch (DWI positive, FLAIR negative), suggesting recent onset (<4.5h).

results.title: Extending the Time for Thrombolysis in Emergency Neurological Deficits (EXTEND Trial)
results.authors: Ma H, Campbell BCV, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase was beneficial in patients 4.5-9 hours from onset or wake-up stroke, selected by perfusion imaging showing salvageable tissue.

results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guideline Update: Wake-up Stroke Management
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: In wake-up stroke patients with DWI-FLAIR mismatch on MRI, IV alteplase can be considered (Class IIa, Level B-R).

output.summary: The WAKE-UP trial (NEJM 2018) established that DWI-FLAIR mismatch can identify wake-up stroke patients who may benefit from IV thrombolysis. Patients with DWI-positive but FLAIR-negative lesions — suggesting onset within approximately 4.5 hours — showed improved functional outcomes with alteplase compared to placebo. When FLAIR is already positive corresponding to the DWI lesion, this suggests the infarct is likely beyond the 4.5-hour window. The EXTEND trial (NEJM 2019) offers an alternative pathway using perfusion imaging to select patients up to 9 hours from onset.

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast head CT MUST exclude intracranial hemorrhage before IV thrombolysis is considered (tPA decision modeled here through drug-interaction/contraindication check).
Glucose, INR/PTT, and platelet count must be reviewed before IV thrombolysis to exclude hypoglycemia mimic and coagulopathy contraindications.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Apply wake-up stroke late-window thrombolysis criteria (DWI-FLAIR mismatch or perfusion mismatch) if imaging supports treatment
Pursue extended cardiac monitoring even with sinus rhythm on initial ECG
Adjust contrast use for CKD stage 3a
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not assume small-vessel mechanism without evaluating large vessels and cardiac source
Do not give iodinated contrast in CKD without hydration or MRA alternative
Avoid order_ct_scan with contrast=True, angiography=True: Iodinated contrast carries elevated nephrotoxicity risk in CKD stage 3a; weigh CTA against MRA alternative and pre-hydrate if necessary
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Subcortical (corona radiata) infarcts can be lacunar OR embolic to a single perforator — vessel imaging and cardiac evaluation are required to assign mechanism reliably
DWI-FLAIR mismatch on MRI is the tissue clock for wake-up presentations
CKD stage 3a requires renal-protective strategy when iodinated contrast is needed
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Non-contrast CT is the required first-line study in the acute window; MRI adds tissue-based selection and is not mandatory for the diagnosis.

clinical_pearls: Wake-up strokes account for approximately 20-25% of all ischemic strokes and require MRI-based selection for thrombolysis eligibility
Left atrial enlargement on ECG in a stroke patient without known AF should always prompt prolonged cardiac monitoring
Approximately 20-30% of initially cryptogenic strokes are found to have paroxysmal AF on prolonged monitoring
The distinction between antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy for secondary prevention is one of the most consequential decisions in stroke management
